steps: Step 1, Proofread in layers. Read this notice once for meaning: 'their is a meeting of the shareholders on monday, all members was requested to attend.' Then hunt by type: spelling and homophones (their/there), capital letters (monday), punctuation (a comma joining two sentences) and agreement (was/were). Mark each error before you correct anything.

Step 2, Correct the errors. 'Their' becomes 'There', because it introduces existence. 'monday' needs a capital: Monday. The comma joins two full sentences, so use a full stop. 'All members was' becomes 'All members were', since 'members' is plural. Result: 'There is a meeting of the shareholders on Monday. All members were requested to attend.'

Step 3, Transform voice. Active: 'The manager approved the budget.' Passive: 'The budget was approved by the manager.' The object moves to the front, the verb becomes was plus the past participle, and the doer follows 'by'. Use the passive in commerce writing when the action matters more than the person: 'Invoices were issued on 5 May.'

Step 4, Transform speech. Direct: The clerk said, 'I will send the invoice tomorrow.' Reported: The clerk said that he would send the invoice the next day. Three changes happen: the quotation marks go, 'will' shifts back to 'would', and 'I' and 'tomorrow' become 'he' and 'the next day'.

Step 5, Combine sentences precisely. 'The firm cut its prices. Sales rose by 12 per cent.' Joined: 'After the firm cut its prices, sales rose by 12 per cent.' Or: 'The firm cut its prices, so sales rose by 12 per cent.' Choose the link that shows the true relationship, here cause and effect, and put a comma after an opening clause.

Step 6, Your turn: edit 'the clerk have posted the invoices yesterday' and then change it to the passive. Answer: Edited: 'The clerk posted the invoices yesterday.' (capital T, and the simple past with 'yesterday', not 'have posted'). Passive: 'The invoices were posted by the clerk yesterday.'

Step 1, Plan a formal complaint letter from facts. Order: 40 office chairs, ordered 3 March, promised for 10 March, delivered 24 March. Lateness is 24 minus 10 = 14 days. Layout: your address, date, the supplier's address, 'Dear Sir or Madam', a subject line, body paragraphs, 'Yours faithfully', your name.

Step 2, Write the opening and the evidence. 'I am writing to complain about the late delivery of 40 office chairs under order 2291. The goods were promised for 10 March but arrived on 24 March, fourteen days late.' Keep the tone formal: no slang, no anger, exact dates and numbers.

Step 3, Persuade with a clear request. 'Our new staff worked without proper seating for two weeks. I therefore request a discount of 10 per cent on the invoice total of 18,000, which is 1,800, so the final amount would be 16,200. Please reply within seven days.' State the remedy, the figure and the deadline.

Step 4, Switch to an analytical report. Use headings: Introduction, Findings, Conclusion, Recommendations. Findings: 'Sales rose from 48,000 in the first quarter to 54,000 in the second, an increase of 6,000, or 12.5 per cent.' Show the figures, then explain what they mean in the Conclusion.

Step 5, Draft a persuasive article opening. 'Can a small shop survive without a website? Of 50 local traders surveyed, 35 (70 per cent) said online orders now bring in a quarter of their income.' A headline, a question, a statistic and a call to action make the writing persuasive.

Step 6, Your turn: write the closing paragraph of a letter asking for a refund of 20 per cent of an 8,000 order. Answer: 20 per cent of 8,000 is 1,600. 'I therefore request a refund of 1,600 within 14 days. I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, [your name]'.

Step 1, Set a time plan before reading. For a 45-minute unseen section: 5 minutes to skim, 30 minutes to answer, 10 minutes to check. Total 5 + 30 + 10 = 45. Passage: 'Ten years ago most market stall owners took only cash. Of 200 owners surveyed, 38 still refuse cards. Supporters of cash call it simple and private; critics call it slow to count and easy to lose.'

Step 2, Skim actively. Read the first and last sentences, circle numbers and underline contrast words such as 'still' and 'critics'. In one line state the main idea: markets are moving from cash to cards, but not every stall has changed. Doing this takes under two minutes and guides every answer.

Step 3, Answer a retrieval question with numbers. 'What proportion of owners still refuse cards?' 38 out of 200 is 19 per cent. The remaining 162 owners, 81 per cent, accept at least one card method. Write the figure and the unit, and quote 'still refuse cards' as proof.

Step 4, Read critically for viewpoint. The writer gives both sides: 'supporters' and 'critics' are placed in balanced clauses of similar length. So the tone is neutral and balanced, not for or against cash. Evidence: neither side is called 'wrong', and no emotive words are used.

Step 5, Use context for vocabulary and summary. 'Refuse' means 'say no to', shown by the contrast with 'accept'. For a 40-word summary, keep only the main idea, the 19 per cent figure and the two opposing views, and leave out examples. Cross out anything you copied word for word.

Step 6, Your turn: give one reason from supporters and one from critics in the passage. Answer: Supporters say cash is simple (or private). Critics say cash is slow to count (or easy to lose). Quote the words 'simple and private' and 'slow to count and easy to lose'.

Step 1, State the shared theme as a sentence. Extract A (prose): 'Amira packed only what the case would hold. At the gate she turned once, and the olive tree seemed to lean toward her.' Extract B (poem): 'I carry the street in my pocket, / its noise folded small.' Theme: leaving home means carrying loss and belonging together.

Step 2, Gather evidence from A. 'Only what the case would hold' shows that leaving forces hard choices. The olive tree 'seemed to lean toward her': personification shows the place itself reluctant to let her go. Write the quotation, then name the technique, then say the effect.

Step 3, Gather evidence from B. 'I carry the street in my pocket' is a metaphor: a whole home shrinks to something portable. 'Its noise folded small' suggests memory has to be made quiet and small to survive in a new place. The speaker is already abroad, so the mood is lonely.

Step 4, Build a comparison grid. Similarity: both treat home as something that cannot be fully packed. Difference: A shows the moment of departure, with the place almost alive, whereas B shows life after arrival, with the place reduced to memory. Use linking words: similarly, whereas, however, in contrast.

Step 5, Write one comparative paragraph. 'Both writers present leaving home as loss. In A, the tree that 'seemed to lean' suggests the homeland resists parting; similarly, in B the street 'folded small' shows memory shrinking. However, A focuses on the departure itself, whereas B reflects on its aftermath.' Quote exactly and compare in each sentence.

Step 6, Your turn: compare 'only what the case would hold' (A) with 'folded small' (B) in two sentences. Model answer: Both phrases show that a whole life must be reduced to fit what can be carried. A's limit is physical, a case, whereas B's is emotional, memory folded small, so A stresses choice and B stresses endurance.

Step 1, State the theme in a sentence. Extract A (prose): 'Ravi lay on the riverbank for an hour, counting the ripples as if they were sums that would one day add up.' Extract B (poem): 'The microscope shows me a drop of pond: / a whole crowded city nobody planned.' Theme: patient looking turns nature into wonder.

Step 2, Gather evidence from A. 'Counting the ripples' shows slow, careful observation, like a scientist taking measurements. The simile 'as if they were sums' links nature with mathematics and suggests Ravi believes the pattern will eventually make sense. 'One hour' shows how patient he is.

Step 3, Gather evidence from B. 'A drop of pond' is tiny, but the metaphor 'a whole crowded city' makes it huge and busy. 'Nobody planned' suggests life organises itself without a designer. The tone is amazed. The microscope, a tool, is what reveals the wonder.

Step 4, Build a comparison grid. Similarity: both characters discover meaning by observing closely. Difference: Ravi observes with his eyes and patience, and still waits for understanding; the speaker uses an instrument and is already astonished. Choose linking words: both, whereas, by contrast.

Step 5, Write one comparative paragraph. 'Both writers show that careful observation reveals order in nature. In A, ripples are 'sums that would one day add up', so understanding is still to come; in B, the pond is already 'a whole crowded city', so wonder is immediate. Both use comparison to make nature feel familiar.'

Step 6, Your turn: compare the simile in A with the metaphor in B in two sentences. Model answer: A's simile 'as if they were sums' makes ripples a puzzle to solve, while B's metaphor 'a crowded city' makes the pond a place to marvel at. Both comparisons turn something small into something full of meaning.

Step 1, Edit for dangling modifiers. 'Walking through the museum, the exhibits impressed us.' The opening phrase must describe the subject, but exhibits cannot walk. Fix: 'Walking through the museum, we were impressed by the exhibits.' Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase, then make that person the subject.

Step 2, Edit punctuation with 'however'. 'The empire grew quickly, however it fell slowly.' A comma cannot join two sentences. Correct: 'The empire grew quickly; however, it fell slowly.' The semicolon links the two ideas, and 'however' takes a comma after it. Alternatively use a full stop before 'However'.

Step 3, Keep tenses consistent. 'In 1948 the delegates signed the charter and celebrations are held across the city.' Both events are in the past, so write 'were held'. Underline every verb in the paragraph, mark its time, and change any that shift without a reason such as a general truth.

Step 4, Repair parallel structure. 'The historian likes reading, to write and researching archives.' The three items must share one form: 'The historian likes reading, writing and researching archives.' Lists, comparisons and 'not only ... but also' pairs all need the same grammatical pattern on each side.

Step 5, Transform a question into reported speech. Direct: She asked, 'Where did the army march?' Reported: She asked where the army had marched. Notice there is no question mark, the word order is statement order, and the past tense shifts back to the past perfect.

Step 6, Your turn: edit 'The council met in March, however nobody agreed' and report 'He asked, 'Why is the bridge closed?'' Answer: 'The council met in March; however, nobody agreed.' Reported: He asked why the bridge was closed.

Step 1, Edit for scientific style. Draft: 'We heated the water to 60 degrees and we wore goggles.' Method sections use the passive and the past tense: 'The water was heated to 60 °C. Safety goggles were worn and the beaker was handled with tongs.' The passive keeps the focus on the procedure, and safety is part of the method.

Step 2, Edit units and numbers. '5ml' becomes '5 mL', with a space and a correct symbol. 'sixty degrees' becomes '60 °C'. Always write the unit once after the number, keep one style throughout, and use figures for measurements. Check each quantity against the data table.

Step 3, Edit agreement and fewer/less. 'The data shows that less samples dissolved.' Formal usage: 'The data show that fewer samples dissolved.' Data is treated as plural in formal science writing, and 'fewer' is used for countable things such as samples, while 'less' is used for uncountable things such as water.

Step 4, Edit certainty. 'This proves that heat speeds up dissolving.' One experiment rarely proves anything, so hedge: 'This suggests that higher temperature increases the rate of dissolving.' Use may, suggests, indicates or is consistent with when the evidence is limited.

Step 5, Transform by combining. 'The solution was stirred. It was left for ten minutes.' Joined: 'The solution was stirred and then left for ten minutes.' Or with a relative clause: 'The solution, which was stirred first, was left for ten minutes.' Pick the version that keeps the order of events clear.

Step 6, Your turn: edit 'We add 5ml of acid and the data shows less bubbles.' Answer: 'Five millilitres of acid were added (or 5 mL of acid was added) and the data show fewer bubbles.' Use the past passive, spell out the number at the start or write the unit with a space, and use 'fewer'. Acid needs goggles and gloves.

Step 1, Plan a letter to the editor. Issue: a plan to close the town library on weekends. Facts: weekly visits are 1,200, and 450 of them happen on Saturday and Sunday, which is 37.5 per cent. Layout: address, date, 'Dear Editor', a subject line, three paragraphs, 'Yours faithfully'.

Step 2, Write the opening and argument. 'I am writing to oppose the plan to close the library at weekends. Of the 1,200 visits made each week, 450, or 37.5 per cent, take place on Saturday and Sunday, when working families can come.' Open with your position, then support it with a figure.

Step 3, Add counter-argument and appeal. 'Some may argue that weekday opening is enough. However, students in school and adults at work cannot use it then.' Answering the opposing view makes the writing persuasive. End: 'I urge the council to keep weekend hours.'

Step 4, Write an analytical report. Survey of 80 students: 56 use the library at least weekly. 56 out of 80 is 70 per cent. Headings: Introduction, Findings, Conclusion, Recommendations. Finding: 'Seventy per cent of students use the library weekly.' Recommendation: extend evening hours.

Step 5, Draft a feature article. Headline: 'Voices Worth Keeping'. Hook: 'Every elder in our village is a living archive.' Develop with a short anecdote, one fact and a quotation, and close with a call to action. Persuasive articles use an engaging headline, vivid detail and a firm final sentence.

Step 6, Your turn: calculate and write one sentence for a report if 18 of 45 residents prefer evening opening. Answer: 18 out of 45 is 40 per cent. 'Forty per cent of the residents surveyed prefer the library to open in the evening, which suggests that evening hours should be considered.'

Step 1, Plan a lab report. Sample data from a class test: time for a spoonful of sugar to dissolve in 100 mL of water was 90 seconds at 20 °C, 55 seconds at 40 °C and 30 seconds at 60 °C. Safety: warm water only, safety goggles, hair tied back, and an adult pours anything hot. Headings: Aim, Method, Results, Conclusion.

Step 2, Write Results analytically. 'As the temperature rose from 20 °C to 60 °C, the dissolving time fell from 90 s to 30 s, a decrease of 60 s or 66.7 per cent.' Quote the figures from the table and describe the trend in one clear sentence before you explain it.

Step 3, Write a hedged conclusion. 'The results suggest that higher temperature shortens the time sugar takes to dissolve, possibly because particles move faster. One trial per temperature limits reliability, so the test should be repeated.' Formal science writing hedges and names a limitation.

Step 4, Write a persuasive letter to a council. 'Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to propose a weekly river-testing project for local schools. Students would measure temperature and clarity, wearing gloves and goggles, and report findings.' State the proposal, the benefit and the safety plan, then close with 'Yours faithfully'.

Step 5, Draft an article for a school magazine. Headline: 'Why Every School Needs a Weather Station'. Hook: 'What if tomorrow's forecast came from your playground?' Add a fact from your records, such as rain on 12 of 30 days (40 per cent), and end with a clear call to action.

Step 6, Your turn: write one results sentence for 25 s at 70 °C compared with 90 s at 20 °C. Answer: The time fell by 65 s, which is 72.2 per cent (65/90). 'Raising the temperature from 20 °C to 70 °C reduced the dissolving time from 90 s to 25 s, a fall of 72.2 per cent.' Hot water needs adult help.

Step 1, Plan the timing. For a 45-minute unseen section, spend 5 minutes skimming, 30 answering and 10 checking. Passage: 'A village project recorded 45 interviews with older residents. Eighteen of the speakers were over 80. The average interview lasted 32 minutes. Some historians doubt memories, yet the project argues that stories reveal what documents omit.'

Step 2, Skim and annotate. Circle the numbers (45, 18, 32), underline 'doubt' and 'yet', and note the main idea: personal memories add something that official records do not, even if they are imperfect. This takes about two minutes and shows the shape of the argument.

Step 3, Answer the number questions. 18 of 45 speakers over 80 is 40 per cent. Total recorded time is 45 x 32 = 1,440 minutes, which is 24 hours. Show the working and add units. Quote 'eighteen' and 'average interview lasted 32 minutes' as evidence.

Step 4, Read critically. 'Some historians doubt memories, yet the project argues...' The word 'yet' signals a counter-claim, and 'argues' presents it as a view, not a fact. A critical reader asks whether the project is neutral. The evidence is one village, so the claim may not apply everywhere.

Step 5, Handle vocabulary and summary. 'Omit' means 'leave out', which the contrast with 'reveal' makes clear. A 35-word summary: 'A village project recorded 45 interviews, 40 per cent with people over 80, arguing that memories show what documents leave out, despite doubts from some historians.' Use your own words.

Step 6, Your turn: state one opposing view in the passage and one limit of the evidence. Answer: Some historians doubt memories (the opposing view). The limit is that the evidence comes from one village, so it may not represent everywhere. Quote 'some historians doubt memories'.

Step 1, Plan the timing. For a 45-minute unseen section, allow 5 minutes to skim, 30 to answer and 10 to check. Passage: 'A school weather station recorded rain on 12 of 30 days. The rainfall total was 96 mm. A student wrote that this clearly proves the town is getting wetter every year.'

Step 2, Skim and mark the claim. Circle 12, 30 and 96 mm, and underline 'clearly proves'. The main idea is that the data are being used to support a strong claim about climate. A scientific reader checks whether thirty days of data can support that claim.

Step 3, Answer with working. Rainy days: 12 out of 30 is 40 per cent. Average rainfall per day: 96 / 30 = 3.2 mm. Average per rainy day: 96 / 12 = 8 mm. Write each answer with its unit, and quote 'rain on 12 of 30 days'.

Step 4, Read critically. 'Clearly proves' is too strong. A single month cannot show a yearly trend; the student would need many years of records for comparison. Fact: 96 mm in 30 days. Opinion or claim: 'wetter every year'. Say so and cite the evidence.

Step 5, Use context for vocabulary and summary. 'Proves' means 'shows beyond doubt', so the writer implies certainty. Summary in 30 words: 'A school weather station recorded rain on 12 of 30 days, totalling 96 mm, but a student wrongly claimed this proves yearly change.' Keep facts and the writer's attitude.

Step 6, Your turn: work out the percentage of dry days and say why the claim is weak. Answer: Dry days are 30 - 12 = 18, which is 60 per cent. The claim is weak because one month of data cannot show a trend across years. 'Proves' is too strong.

Step 1, Look at one sentence: 'I am Sam.' It starts with a big letter, a capital letter: I. It ends with a dot, a full stop. Say the sentence. Then point to the capital letter and point to the full stop. A name like Sam also has a capital letter at the start.

Step 2, Copy a sentence slowly: 'The cat is big.' Start with a capital T. Leave a small space between each word (use one finger). Write the full stop at the end. Say each word as you write it. Copy the sentence three times on your page.

Step 3, Fix a sentence. Wrong: the dog is red. Right: The dog is red. Change t to T and add a full stop. Another one. Wrong: i like milk. Right: I like milk. The word I is always a capital letter. Fix both sentences in your book.

Step 4, Put the words in order. Words: is / My / happy / mum. Sentence: My mum is happy. Check three things: a capital M at the start, the words in the right order, and a full stop at the end. Read the sentence aloud and listen to it.

Step 5, Write three sentences about you. My name is Ana. I am nine. I like rice. Each sentence has a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end. The name Ana has a capital A. Now write your own three sentences.
Step 6, Your turn: fix this sentence: we have a ball. Answer: We have a ball. (Capital W at the start and a full stop at the end.)

Step 1, Read the whole text once for the general idea. Text: 'Mia has a small garden. She grows tomatoes and beans. Every morning she gives them water. In summer the garden is full of red tomatoes. Mia shares them with her neighbours.' Do not stop at hard words. Ask: who is this about, and what is happening?

Step 2, Find the main idea. The main idea is what the whole text is about. Here the text is about Mia and her garden. Main idea: Mia grows vegetables in her garden and shares them. Check: does every sentence fit this idea? Yes, so it is a good main idea.

Step 3, Find the details. Details give small facts. Who? Mia. What does she grow? Tomatoes and beans. When does she water the plants? Every morning. Underline each answer in the text with a pencil, then write the answer in a short note in your book.

Step 4, Use question words to check. Who? What? When? Where? Why? Question: What does Mia do with the tomatoes? Look back and find the sentence: 'Mia shares them with her neighbours.' Answer: She shares them with her neighbours. Always look back at the text for the answer.

Step 5, Decide true or false. Sentence: 'Mia grows carrots.' The text says tomatoes and beans, so the sentence is false. Sentence: 'Mia waters her plants every morning.' This is true. Write T or F, and write the line from the text that proves it.

Step 6, Your turn: write the main idea and one detail. Answer: Main idea: Mia has a garden and grows vegetables. Detail: She waters the plants every morning. (Another good detail: she shares tomatoes with her neighbours.)

Step 1, Choose a topic and think of ideas. Topic: My Saturday. Write a quick list: help at home, wash dishes, play football, read a book, go to bed. Choose four ideas for your paragraph. A paragraph is a group of sentences about one topic, and you need five connected sentences.

Step 2, Write sentence 1, the topic sentence. It says what the paragraph is about. 'On Saturday I help at home and I have fun.' Begin with a capital letter, and end with a full stop. Keep it short, and make sure it matches your list of ideas.

Step 3, Write sentences 2 to 4 with linking words. 'First, I wash the dishes. Next, I play football with my friend. Then I read a book.' The words first, next and then show the order of events. After the linking word at the start, put a comma, except after 'then'.

Step 4, Write sentence 5, the ending. 'Finally, I go to bed at nine.' Together: 1 topic sentence, 2 first, 3 next, 4 then, 5 finally. Count the sentences: five. Read all five aloud. Do they follow one after another and make sense?

Step 5, Check your work. Does each sentence start with a capital letter and end with a full stop? Are the verbs all present simple (help, wash, play)? Is the spelling right? Are there five sentences? Fix one mistake and rewrite neatly.
Step 6, Your turn: write five connected sentences about My School Day. Model answer: I like my school day. First, I read in class. Next, I play with my friends. Then I do maths. Finally, I walk home.

Step 1, Ask for help politely. 'Excuse me, can you help me, please?' Use 'Excuse me' to get attention, and 'please' to be polite. Add the problem: 'I do not understand question three.' Speak clearly, look at the teacher, and wait for the answer before you write.

Step 2, Ask about words. 'What does "measure" mean?' 'How do you spell "triangle"?' 'Can you give me an example, please?' These three questions help you learn new subject words. Write the answer in your notebook with the word, meaning and a short example sentence.

Step 3, Ask someone to repeat. 'Could you say that again, please?' 'Could you speak more slowly?' Say these when the teacher speaks too fast. It is not rude to ask. Then listen to the answer and repeat the key words: 'Page twelve. Question three.'

Step 4, Follow subject instructions in order. 'Open your book to page 12. Read the first paragraph. Underline the verbs. Then write two sentences.' Number the actions 1, 2, 3, 4 in your notebook. Instruction words are verbs at the start: open, read, underline, write.

Step 5, Check you understand. Say: 'So I read first, then underline the verbs, and then write two sentences. Is that correct?' The teacher says yes or corrects you. This checking sentence saves time and stops mistakes before you start the task.
Step 6, Your turn: you do not understand 'Circle the nouns.' What do you say? Model answer: 'Excuse me, what does "noun" mean? Could you give me an example, please?'

Step 1, Read the text for the general idea. 'Water changes form. When the sun heats a lake, some water evaporates: it becomes a gas called water vapour. High in the sky the vapour cools and condenses into tiny drops. The drops make clouds. When the drops are heavy, they fall as rain.' Main idea: how water moves from the lake to the sky and back.

Step 2, List the key words. Evaporate: change from liquid to gas. Water vapour: water as a gas. Condense: change from gas to liquid. Cloud: many tiny water drops in the sky. Write each word, its meaning and one picture or example in your word book.

Step 3, Put the process in order with arrows. Sun heats the lake, then water evaporates, then vapour rises, then it cools and condenses, then clouds form, then rain falls. Number the steps 1 to 6. Use time words: first, then, next, finally.

Step 4, See condensation safely. A cold glass of water on a warm day gets drops on the outside. Water vapour from the air touches the cold glass and condenses. This is safe, with no heat. Never touch steam from a kettle: steam burns, so only an adult should boil water.

Step 5, Answer questions with the text. What makes water evaporate? The heat of the sun. What is water vapour? Water as a gas. What happens when drops become heavy? They fall as rain. Look back at the text and answer in a full sentence.
Step 6, Your turn: complete: 'Vapour ___ and becomes tiny drops.' Answer: condenses (or cools and condenses). It is the opposite of 'evaporates', so it changes from a gas to a liquid.

Step 1, Read for characters and setting. Story: 'Lena found a small kite in a tree. It was torn. She took it home and fixed it with tape. The next day she flew it in the park. A boy, Omar, laughed and said, "That is my kite!" Lena gave it back, and Omar taught her to fly it.' Characters: Lena and Omar. Setting: a tree, Lena's home, the park.

Step 2, Find the beginning, middle and end. Beginning: Lena finds a torn kite. Middle: she fixes it and flies it in the park, and Omar says it is his. End: Lena gives the kite back and Omar teaches her to fly it. Write one short line for each part.

Step 3, Notice the past tense verbs. found, was, took, fixed, flew, said, gave, taught. Some verbs are regular and end in -ed (fixed, laughed). Others are irregular (find to found, take to took, fly to flew, give to gave, teach to taught). Learn the irregular ones as a list.

Step 4, Choose time words for your retelling. First, then, the next day, after that, finally. Example: 'First, Lena found a torn kite. Then she fixed it with tape.' Time words show the order. Say each sentence aloud before you write it.

Step 5, Retell in your own words. 'Lena found a torn kite in a tree and fixed it. The next day she flew it in the park. Omar said it was his kite, so Lena gave it back. Finally, Omar taught her to fly it.' That is four sentences with no extra detail.
Step 6, Your turn: answer, 'Why did Lena give the kite back?' Model answer: Lena gave the kite back because it was Omar's kite. (She was kind, so Omar taught her to fly it.)

Step 1, Make the present perfect. Form: have or has + past participle. 'I have finished my homework.' 'She has eaten lunch.' Use it for something that happened at an unfinished time or whose result matters now. Irregular participles: be, been; see, seen; do, done; eat, eaten.

Step 2, Use for and since. 'For' + a length of time; 'since' + a starting point. 'I have lived here for three years.' 'I have lived here since 2023.' Today is in 2026, so 2026 - 2023 = 3. Both sentences are true together. Choose for or since correctly in each sentence.

Step 3, Add ever, never, already and yet. 'Have you ever visited a museum?' 'I have never seen snow.' 'He has already finished.' 'She has not finished yet.' Ever and never go between have and the participle; yet goes at the end of a negative or question sentence.

Step 4, Use the first conditional for real future possibilities. Form: If + present simple, will + base verb. 'If it rains, we will stay inside.' 'If you study, you will pass.' Do not use 'will' after if. Wrong: If it will rain. Right: If it rains.

Step 5, Use the zero conditional for facts. Form: If + present simple, present simple. 'If you heat ice, it melts.' 'If you mix red and yellow, you get orange.' Compare: 'If you heat the ice' (a general fact) and 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay in' (one future event).
Step 6, Your turn: complete: 'I ___ (live) here since 2021' and 'If it ___ (be) hot tomorrow, we ___ (go) swimming.' Answer: I have lived here since 2021. If it is hot tomorrow, we will go swimming.

Step 1, Prepare your opinion. Topic: Should our class have a school garden? Write one opinion and one reason. 'I think we should have a garden because we can grow vegetables.' Write it in note form and practise it aloud twice. A reason makes your opinion strong.

Step 2, Start and invite your partner. 'I think we should have a garden because it is good for the environment. What do you think?' Say your opinion in one or two sentences, then ask a question. This gives your partner a turn and keeps the discussion fair.

Step 3, Agree and disagree politely. 'I agree with you, because plants need care and we can share the work.' 'I see your point, but we do not have much space.' Use 'I agree', 'I see your point, but', or 'I am not sure, because'. Never say 'You are wrong'.

Step 4, Repair when you do not understand. 'Sorry, could you say that again?' 'What do you mean by "space"?' 'Do you mean the school yard?' These questions are part of good speaking. Listen to the answer and use one of the partner's words in your reply.

Step 5, Finish the discussion. 'So we both think a garden is a good idea, but we need a plan for space and water.' A closing sentence summarises the shared view and one problem. Say 'Thank you for your ideas' and smile.
Step 6, Your turn: respond to 'I think we should have homework on Fridays.' Model answer: I see your point, but I think we need Fridays to rest, because we work hard all week. What do you think?

Step 1, Preview the text. Text: 'Bees are important for food. Many crops, such as apples and almonds, need pollinators to make fruit and seeds. Scientists estimate that about one third of the food people eat depends on animal pollination. However, bee numbers have fallen in some regions because of habitat loss and pesticides. Planting flowers can help.' Read the title and first sentence first.

Step 2, Find the main idea. The first sentence often gives it: 'Bees are important for food.' Check the other sentences. They explain why (crops need pollinators), a problem (fewer bees) and a solution (plant flowers). So the main idea is that bees matter for our food, and they need protection.

Step 3, Find the evidence. Evidence supports the main idea with facts. Evidence 1: apples and almonds need pollinators. Evidence 2: about one third of our food depends on animal pollination. Underline both in two colours: one for examples, one for numbers or estimates.

Step 4, Notice signal words. 'However' marks a contrast: after good news about bees, the text gives a problem. 'Because of' introduces causes: habitat loss and pesticides. 'Can help' introduces a solution. Signal words show how ideas connect, so circle each one.

Step 5, Take notes in your own words. Main idea: bees help produce food. Evidence: apples, almonds, one third of food. Problem: fewer bees, because of lost habitat and pesticides. Solution: plant flowers. Use short phrases, not full sentences, and do not copy long parts of the text.

Step 6, Your turn: give the main idea and one piece of evidence from the text. Answer: Main idea: bees are important for our food. Evidence: about one third of the food people eat depends on animal pollination (or apples and almonds need pollinators).

Step 1, Choose a claim for one paragraph. Topic: Students should read for 20 minutes every day. Use the TEEL structure: Topic sentence, Explanation, Evidence, Link. Write each letter in the margin to plan the paragraph before you write any full sentences.

Step 2, Write the topic sentence and explanation. 'Students should read for twenty minutes every day. Regular reading builds vocabulary and improves concentration, which helps students in every subject.' The topic sentence states the claim. The explanation gives the reason.

Step 3, Add evidence. 'Twenty minutes a day is 7,300 minutes in a year (20 x 365), which is more than 120 hours of reading.' Then link: 'Therefore, a short daily habit gives students a large amount of practice.' Use numbers carefully, and check the arithmetic.

Step 4, Plan a short essay of five paragraphs. Introduction with a thesis, two body paragraphs (TEEL each), a counter-argument paragraph, and a conclusion. Thesis: 'Daily reading helps students learn, so schools should protect time for it.' Use linking words such as firstly, in addition and therefore.

Step 5, Write the conclusion and check. 'In conclusion, daily reading improves vocabulary and builds a habit that lasts. Schools should therefore give time for it.' Do not add new evidence. Check: topic sentences, capital letters, full stops, linking words and one idea per paragraph.

Step 6, Your turn: write a TEEL paragraph about 'Students should drink water at school.' Model answer: Students should drink water at school. Water helps the body and brain work well. For example, one bottle of 500 mL is easy to carry. Therefore, water keeps students ready to learn.

Step 1, Learn maths words with an example. For 12 and 4: sum = 12 + 4 = 16; difference = 12 - 4 = 8; product = 12 x 4 = 48; quotient = 12 / 4 = 3. Say a full sentence: 'The product of 12 and 4 is 48.' Write each term with its operation in a table.

Step 2, Use shape words in a task. A rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Area = length x width = 6 x 4 = 24 cm squared. Perimeter = 2 x (6 + 4) = 20 cm. Perimeter is the distance around the shape; area is the space inside.

Step 3, Learn science measuring words. Mass is how much matter an object has (grams). Volume is the space it takes (millilitres). To measure 50 mL of water, put a measuring cylinder on a flat table and read the scale at eye level, at the bottom of the curved surface.

Step 4, Learn action words for experiments. Dissolve: sugar dissolves in water. Evaporate: water evaporates when heated. Observe, record, compare. Safety: wear goggles when heating, wipe spills at once so nobody slips, and ask a teacher before using hot water.

Step 5, Follow an instruction and report it. 'Measure 50 mL of water, add one spoon of salt, stir, and record what you observe.' Report: 'The salt dissolved in the water. I observed that the water stayed clear.' Use past tense for what you did and observed.
Step 6, Your turn: a rectangle is 5 cm by 3 cm. Give the area and perimeter in a sentence. Answer: The area is 15 cm squared (5 x 3) and the perimeter is 16 cm (2 x (5 + 3)).

Step 1, Learn social studies words. Population: the number of people living in a place. Government: the group that makes decisions for a country. Economy: how money, work and goods are made and shared. Climate: usual weather over many years. Write each word with a short example sentence about your own region.

Step 2, Use a number task. Population density is population divided by area. A town has 6,000 people and an area of 3 square kilometres. 6,000 / 3 = 2,000 people per square kilometre. Say: 'The population density is 2,000 people per square kilometre.' Use 'per' for rates.

Step 3, Use map words. A map key explains symbols, and a scale shows real distance. If 1 cm on the map is 5 km, then 4 cm is 4 x 5 = 20 km. Say: 'The distance between the two towns is 20 kilometres.' Use compass directions: north, south, east, west.

Step 4, Learn computing words. A file is one saved document. A folder holds files. A password protects an account, and you should never share it. An algorithm is a list of steps to solve a problem. Input is the data you give; output is the result you get.

Step 5, Read a tiny program. age = 12 / if age >= 10: / print('junior'). The program stores 12 in age, tests if age is at least 10, and prints junior, so the output is: junior. Explain: 'If the condition is true, the computer runs the next line.'
Step 6, Your turn: a village has 900 people and covers 2 square kilometres. Say the density. Answer: 900 / 2 = 450, so the population density is 450 people per square kilometre.

Step 1, Plan the structure. A short talk has three parts: introduction, main points, conclusion. Topic: Why I recycle. Plan two main points: it saves materials and it reduces waste. A three-minute talk at about 120 words a minute is around 360 words, so choose only two or three ideas.

Step 2, Open clearly. 'Good morning, everyone. My name is Sara, and today I will talk about recycling. I will give two reasons: it saves materials and it reduces waste.' Greet, introduce yourself, say the topic and tell the audience what is coming.

Step 3, Signpost the main points. 'My first point is that recycling saves materials.' 'Now I will move to my second point.' 'In conclusion, recycling is easy and useful.' Signpost phrases help the audience follow you. Look at the audience, speak slowly and pause after each point.

Step 4, Use a visual simply. Put one picture or three key words on each slide, not a whole paragraph. Point to the slide: 'As you can see here, a bottle can be reused.' Do not read from the slide. Practise your talk aloud twice, and time it.

Step 5, Respond to questions. 'Thank you for your question.' 'Good question. I think...' If you do not understand: 'Could you repeat that, please?' If you do not know: 'I am not sure, but I can find out.' Keep answers short, polite and honest.

Step 6, Your turn: write an opening and a closing for a talk about school sport. Model answer: Good morning, everyone. Today I will talk about school sport. In conclusion, sport keeps us healthy and teaches teamwork. Thank you. Are there any questions?
